senses: An online video broadcast in which a person eats.
ety: Borrowed from Korean 먹방 (meokbang, literally “eating broadcast”).
examples: I also get the sense, though, that some of those who, for whatever reason, often end up eating alone are tuning in for a dose of mukbang at mealtimes to get some virtual company (see the “Social Dining” chapter).
I eat the pussy like a mukbang, let my nuts hang

senses: The tendency for a person to act without reference to others, particularly in matters of style, fashion or mode of thought.
The doctrine that nothing exists but the individual self.
ety: Borrowed from French individualisme, equivalent to individual + -ism.
examples: He believes that self-improvement and its growing popularity are symptoms of what he calls individualism.

senses: A road, route, or passage used for travelling over or through.
ety: From Middle English farewaye, fairway, fare-waye, from Old English færweġ (“a cartroad”), from Proto-West Germanic *faraweg, *faruweg (“fareway”), equivalent to fare (“travel”) + way. Cognate with West Frisian farwei (“waterway”), Dutch vaarweg (“waterway”), Middle Low German vārwech, vaerwech (“fareway”), German Fahrweg (“fareway”).
examples: He spoke of his several forefathers' experience at expanding the Far Fleets, which rendered safe all fareways running between the Attican Peninsula and all southerly depots that had been mentioned.
The others parted their ships asunder, and made a fareway between the ships.

senses: Having lungs (of a specified type).
ety: From lung + -ed.
examples: He had grown a big strong fellow, but I had no difficulty in identifying the little squinting child, who begged, and sold flowers and songs in public-house bars, with the strong loud-lunged vendor of mackerel.

senses: In a good mood; happy and energetic.
Making chirping noises.
ety: From chirp + -y.
examples: He's surprisingly chirpy for someone who just lost his father.

Judging by the new voice over the PA, we've had a crew change in Plymouth - the warning about masks and the apology for lack of catering is made in a chirpy Cockney twang rather than a West Country burr.

senses: To make smarter in appearance; to refurbish or spruce up.
To increase the speed of (one's travel on foot, etc.).
To augment with computer technology.
ety: From smart + -en.
examples: The Sorting Ceremony will take place in a few minutes in front of the rest of the school. I suggest you all smarten yourselves up as much as you can while you are waiting.
I braced myself and smartened my pace, shouldering my way through the crowd.

How do we achieve this smartening of the grid? The CALM approach in the future will be to use reinforcement learning (RL) controllers as a basis for optimizing the synergy between operators and automation.

senses: A fried corn or flour tortilla, filled usually with beef or chicken and cheese, rolled up, and dipped in a form of salsa, or guacamole.
ety: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish taquito (literally “little taco”).
examples: She preferred taquitos to regular tacos because she found them less messy.

senses: The (therapeutic) use of electricity directly applied to the body.
ety: From French galvanisme, after physiologist Luigi Alyisio Galvani (1737–1798) + -isme. By surface analysis, galvano- + -ism.
examples: Perhaps a corpse would be re-animated; galvanism had given token of such things: perhaps the component parts of a creature might be manufactured, brought together, and endued with vital warmth.
The sudden application of galvanism to bands of savages may fairly rank as a new sensation, and they, thinking the wire held this strange and mysterious power, wisely left it alone.
Erb and Remak in Germany, Beard and Rockwell and Althans in America, have used it with advantage, in the forms of galvanisms and faradisms, in the treatment of joint troubles.

senses: A gathering or event at which people sleep outdoors or camp.
ety: Deverbal from camp out.
examples: Circle the words that would be good to use in a story titled "The Scariest Campout Ever!"

Even if you have a whole week of vacation and not just a short weekend, for your first campout with small children you are better off planning a trip of only one or two nights until you get the hang of camping.

senses: To scrape the feet while walking.
To scrape and roughen the surface of (shoes, etc.)
To hit lightly, to brush against.
To mishit (a shot on a ball) due to poor contact with the ball.
ety: From Scots scuff (“to touch lightly, graze, hit”), of obscure origin. Perhaps from Old Norse skúfa (“to shove, push aside”), from Proto-Germanic *skeubaną (“to shove”). Or, perhaps imitative. More at shove.
examples: The lawns and gardens had been scuffed away.
Wallace threw himself at it to connect with a flying header. He looked a certain scorer but his effort scuffed the inside of Fraser Forster’s post.
The Montenegro captain was finding space at will and followed up with a speculative shot that he scuffed wide, after Wales were slow in closing down the Juventus striker.

senses: To make something into a problem.
To consider something as if it were a problem.
To propose problems.
ety: From Ancient Greek πρόβλημα, προβλήματος (próblēma, problḗmatos) + English -ize.
examples: Dr Allen said it could affect social cohesion and potentially drive harmful rhetoric around migration when Australia's population change was problematised.

senses: A playful leap or jump.
A jump while dancing.
A prank or practical joke.
Playful behaviour.
A crime, especially an elaborate heist, or a narrative about such a crime.
ety: Clipping of capriole.
examples: His caper had failed to find a comic resolution. Instead, there had been a genre switch, and the madcap adventure had turned serious. Or had this bleakness underlain the caper from the start?

senses: A computer floppy disk of the kind supplied in a stiff plastic outer shell.
A rigidly conformative person; a square or goody-goody.
ety: From stiff + -y.
examples: Never leave home without a spare stiffy disc in your bag.

senses: Sand or similar particulate material suspended in water or other fluid and used in hydraulic fracturing (fracking) to keep fissures open.
ety: From prop + -ant.
examples: The use of resin coated proppants is an area that should increase the chance of success of fracturing for sand control by eliminating the chance for proppant to flow out of the fracture.

senses: A tithe or tax of one-tenth (now usually in historical Italian contexts).
An organ stop a tenth above the normal 8-foot pitch.
ety: Borrowed from Latin decima (“a tenth”), now particularly via Italian decima. Doublet of decim, decime, and dime.
examples: He brandished his title as apostolic commissioner in court, and as supervisor of the papal decima in Tuscany.

senses: A folk dance of the Levant.
ety: Borrowed from North Levantine Arabic دَبْكة (dabka) and South Levantine Arabic دَبْكة (dabke).
examples: My wife is Jordanian and has family who have lived and worked in Dubai and Abu Dhabi for years. During our time in the U.A.E., we ate with them, drank arak, watched them dance the dabke late into the evening.

senses: Exhibiting or relating to ableism.
ety: From able + -ist, by analogy with racist, sexist, etc.
examples: The words "lame" and "spaz" are ableist slurs.
Beyoncé’s commitment to musical and visual storytelling did not “excuse her use of ableist language – language that gets used and ignored all too often”, wrote Diviney.

senses: An area of cultivated ground; a plot of land, a small subsistence farm for growing crops and fruit-bearing trees, often including the dwelling of the farmer.
ety: From Swahili shamba.
examples: To reach his new strip of shamba which lay the other side of Thabai, Mugo had to walk through the dusty village streets.

senses: The conviction that it is morally wrong to settle disputes (especially between countries) by war or other violent means.
The ethical avoidance of inflicting harm on others in one's daily life.
The combination of the above two philosophical viewpoints.
The additional challenge of winning a game without harming any enemy characters.
ety: From French pacifisme, from pacifique; pacific + -ism.
examples: I am not only a pacifist but a militant pacifist. I am willing to fight for peace. Nothing will end war unless the people themselves refuse to go to war.

senses: The amount or proportion of something that is wasted or lost by deterioration or other natural process.
The periodical turnover of personnel in an organisation by death, retirement or resignation, as perceived by those aspiring to promotion or appointment in the organisation.
Anything lost by wear or waste.
Goods that are damaged, out of date, reduced, or generally unsaleable, which are destined to be thrown away and which are written off as a loss.
The act of abandoning animal carcasses or parts, usually illegal.
ety: From waste + -age.
examples: The average wastage is 1.5% in the grocery department.

Likewise, the menopause market is obsessed with muscle wastage, and the possibility that if women don't eat enough protein after the age of 40 their minds will go doolally and their bones will turn to dust.

senses: To needlessly destroy or deface other people’s property or public property; to commit vandalism.
ety: From vandal + -ise.
examples: Unfortunately, one side of the new five-car train is daubed in graffiti, having been vandalised in Wembley Yard, en route from Switzerland.

senses: A silver coin in Ancient Greece, equivalent to four drachms.
ety: From Ancient Greek τετράδραχμον (tetrádrakhmon). See tetra- (“four”).
examples: The dealer gave the coin a moment's scrutiny. "There is no question about this," he replied. "It is a Sicilian tetradrachm of Dionysius."

senses: Prone to glitches.
Characteristic of glitch or error.
ety: From glitch + -y.
examples: The output of a multiplexer can also be glitchy due to the propagation of glitches from the data and select inputs.
If the phone is still glitchy, try to remember what changes you made to it recently. Did you install some new App Store program, add a new video, mess around with your calendar?
The unprecedented move comes one day after Samsung halted production of the dangerously glitchy devices.

senses: A person who takes a mechanical view; someone who subscribes to mechanism.
ety: From mechanism + -ist.
examples: The economic spirit of a people cannot be manipulated in as simple-minded a fashion as the Keynesian mechanists imagine.

senses: A person who aids or assists.
ety: From aid + -er.
examples: The woman in question had, as she said, been a close friend of Margaret’s, and, as such, an aider in her habits of intemperance.

senses: A type of long-necked gazelle, Litocranius walleri, native to central and eastern Africa.
ety: From Somali garanuug.
examples: Unaccountably, he finds himself thinking of gerenuks and gazelles.
She was beautiful, sloe black eyes and red ripe lips atop the long neck of a gerenuk, her pure brown skin set off by yards of carnelian and amber beads;

senses: Any online lexicon resembling Wiktionary, often one that can be freely edited.
ety: From Wiktionary, a blend of wiki + dictionary.
examples: However, with the increase in free resources like wiktionaries, or the increase in the number of translated materials available on the Internet

PanLex draws on various lexical resources, including dictionaries, wiktionaries, glossaries, lexicons, word lists, terminologies, thesauri, wordnets, ontologies, vocabulary databases, namedentity resources, and standards

senses: Speech or writing that is unintelligible, incoherent or meaningless.
ety: First attested mid-16th century. Origin obscure. Possibly from *gibber, of onomatopoeic origin imitating to the sound of chatter, possibly from or influenced by jabber, + -ish denoting the name of a language (compare English, Finnish, Spanish, etc.). The verb gibber, first attested circa 1600, is usually regarded as a back-formation from gibberish.
examples: Such gibberish as children may be heard amusing themselves with.

senses: A recreational or medical cannabis dispensary worker who sells marijuana and is knowledgeable about various cannabis products.
ety: Blend of bud + bartender.
examples: The so-called budtenders who work behind large glass display cases provide assistance in selecting the best strain. All of them are medical marijuana users, and they typically are medicated while working.
Oak Peak is a “budtender” at the Giving Tree of Denver, a marijuana dispensary that sells such edibles as Karma Kandy.

senses: Having ears (of a specified type).
Having ears.
ety: From ear + -ed.
examples: He might have flinched altogether from speaking if at this moment he had not seen Ampleforth, the hairy-eared poet, wandering limply round the room with a tray, looking for a place to sit down.

senses: Hermetic philosophy or practice; hermetics.
ety: From hermetic + -ism.
examples: Yet the old tradition of the spiritual quest, reinforced by the influence of Renaissance hermeticism, could still capture the imagination of highly religious persons.

senses: The lining of the large stomach of ruminating animals, when prepared for food.
The entrails; (by extension, humorous or derogatory) the belly.
An edible lichen, especially rock tripe.
ety: From Middle English tripe, from Old French tripe (“entrails”), of uncertain origin; possibly borrowed from Spanish tripa.
examples: You saw only your mother die. I see them pop off every day in the Mater and Richmond and cut up into tripes in the dissectingroom.
Tripe: A popular dish commonly believed to be a sexual stimulant.
Next morning Miss Dolly complained of her Tripes; / Drinking cold water had given her gripes.

senses: Capable of being penetrated, entered, or pierced.
Capable of being fully understood.
ety: From Middle English penetrable, penytrable, from Old French penetrable, from Medieval Latin penetrābilis.
examples: On the east the high mountain-chain of Zagros, penetrable only in one or two places, forms a barrier of the most marked character, and is beyond a doubt the natural limit for which we are looking.
A Boer may know you, but it will take you some time to know him, and when a certain stage in your acquaintance is reached, you may begin to wonder whether his real nature is penetrable at all.
A capacity is cognitively penetrable in this sense if that capacity is affected by the subject's knowledge or ignorance of the domain.

senses: To convene, to cause to assemble for a meeting.
To call together.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French convoquer, from Latin convocare, from con- (“with”) + vocō (“to call”). Doublet of convocate.
examples: The dream makes such an impression on the king that he convokes his council of state, whose members are thoroughly alarmed by his report.

senses: Food or fodder, particularly that taken in by plants or animals.
Material that feeds a fire.
Food for thought.
Bland intellectual fare; an undemanding diet of words.
ety: Borrowed from Latin pābulum (“food, nourishment; fodder or pasture for animals; nourishment for the mind, food for thought”), from pā(scō) (“to nourish”) + -bulum (suffix denoting an instrument), or directly from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-dʰlom (*peh₂- (“to protect, shepherd”) + *-dʰlom, variant of *-trom (suffix denoting a tool or instrument)).
examples: And with the eye of a bird seeking for minute fragmnts of seed, minute insects, tiny parasites, we also look for things that to us are the constituents of our mental or visual pabula.
But the rescheduling of the directors' meeting for 7.30 a.m., and the trotting-out of such tawdry pabulums?
As this was largely a traditionally crafted speech, there were some painful cliches and political pabulum to which a typical politician might be prone, of course.

senses: An avalanche, mudslide, or a like slumping of material or debris.
ety: From Middle English slough (“skin, husk, rind; cocoon; scales; cyst”), akin to Middle High German slûch (“slough”) (whence German Schlauch (“tube, hose”)).
examples: At least for small sluffs like the ones Brown and his colleagues have triggered, the avalanche slides like a block of material instead of flowing like a fluid.

senses: A smooth, gliding transition from one note to another; used especially with stringed instruments, and sometimes on brass.
ety: From Italian portamento, from portare (“bear, carry”).
examples: The music was feral, Eastern in scale, flattened seconds and sixths, and a kind of fretless portamento between

senses: Makeup, cosmetics, or its application, especially in theatrical or excessive use.
ety: Borrowed from French maquillage.
examples: The ladies of his court – and plenty of the men too – adapted their maquillage to take advantage of artificial lighting to draw attention to their rosy cheeks, white bosoms, jet black eyebrows and scarlet lips.

senses: A Latin American drug baron, usually from Colombia or Mexico.
ety: Clipping of narcotics. From narcotic.
examples: The conflict has become a test of endurance for both the government and the narcos.

senses: That operates by squirting.
Reminiscent of squirting (especially of sound)
ety: From squirt + -y.
examples: The woman was busy making the hot chocolates; she was now bent down retrieving the squirty cream from a small box fridge nestled underneath the counter.
